Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "i went to the archaeology museum on a rainy saturday with my sister lena and my nephew theo, who is nine. we had planned to spend an hour there, mostly because theo had been studying ancient cities at school, but we stayed until the afternoon. the museum is in an old brick building near the river, and the first thing we noticed was a line of wet umbrellas leaning in a brass stand by the entrance. a volunteer at the desk gave us a folded map and said the upstairs galleries were quieter if we wanted to start there. we started downstairs instead, because theo saw a large stone doorway through the glass doors and wanted to know if it was real.

section one, the harbor room. this was the part i liked best. there was a long glass case with a ship model, fishing weights, broken amphora handles, and a bronze pin shaped like a fish. the model had a high curved front and a flat deck, and a note said it represented a boat used to carry grain between ports. a recording played the sound of waves and ropes creaking, but it was quiet enough that we could still hear people speaking nearby. theo asked whether the sailors had maps, and a museum guide named marion told him they probably used landmarks and knowledge passed between crews. she said, quote, the sea could look familiar one morning and completely different by afternoon, end quote. theo nodded as if this settled the matter. beside the model, a tablet showed the outline of a harbor with three small buildings. the guide pointed out a line of stones where workers had repaired the edge after a storm. i liked that detail because it made the place seem less like a picture in a book and more like somewhere people had to maintain.

2. the workshop table. near the back of the gallery, a low display case held tools that had been found together in a small workshop. there was a stone weight, two iron blades, a wooden handle, and several tiny scraps of metal. the label said the scraps might have been left over from repairs, though it also said the exact work done there was uncertain. i appreciated that they did not pretend to know more than the evidence showed. theo used the map to find the family house again, then spotted a symbol beside it that meant there was a touchable replica. the replica was a clay bowl with ridges around its edge. he turned it over carefully and said it felt heavier than he expected. a staff member told us it had been made from a scan of the original, so visitors could handle it without risking damage.

new paragraph we stopped in the small cafe around one o'clock. i had tea and a cheese sandwich, lena had soup, and theo chose a biscuit shaped like a dinosaur even though there were no dinosaurs in the museum. from the table we could see the courtyard, where rainwater was collecting in a shallow channel beside a row of stones. after lunch we went back to the harbor room because theo wanted to hear the recording once more. a toddler nearby kept saying boat, boat, and his father answered, yes, a very old boat. that made us laugh softly. before we left, i bought a postcard of the painted fragments and lena bought a pencil for theo. we had planned to stay an hour, but we had spent nearly four, and none of us felt rushed. on the walk back to the bus stop, theo told us his favorite thing was the bowl because it was the only object he could touch. mine was the harbor model, and lena said hers was the doorway. we agreed the museum had made an ordinary family visit feel like a small journey, though we were all glad to get out of the rain.", "output": "I went to the archaeology museum on a rainy Saturday with my sister Lena and my nephew Theo, who is nine. We had planned to spend an hour there, mostly because Theo had been studying ancient cities at school, but we stayed until the afternoon. The museum is in an old brick building near the river, and the first thing we noticed was a line of wet umbrellas leaning in a brass stand by the entrance. A volunteer at the desk gave us a folded map and said the upstairs galleries were quieter if we wanted to start there. We started downstairs instead, because Theo saw a large stone doorway through the glass doors and wanted to know if it was real.

The doorway came from a house excavated near the coast, and a small sign explained that it had been moved in sections and rebuilt inside the museum. The blocks were rough and pale, with dark marks along the lower edge. Theo asked if people had walked through it every day, and Lena read the label aloud, which said the house was used by a family of merchants about two thousand years ago. I had thought the museum would mostly have pots and coins, but the first room also had a wooden ladder, a bowl of dried dates, and a clay tablet with a list of deliveries. One of the deliveries was olive oil. The tablet was displayed at an angle under a soft light, and I had to lean close to read the translation.

1. The harbor room. This was the part I liked best. There was a long glass case with a ship model, fishing weights, broken amphora handles, and a bronze pin shaped like a fish. The model had a high curved front and a flat deck, and a note said it represented a boat used to carry grain between ports. A recording played the sound of waves and ropes creaking, but it was quiet enough that we could still hear people speaking nearby. Theo asked whether the sailors had maps, and a museum guide named Marion told him they probably used landmarks and knowledge passed between crews. She said, “The sea could look familiar one morning and completely different by afternoon.” Theo nodded as if this settled the matter. Beside the model, a tablet showed the outline of a harbor with three small buildings. The guide pointed out a line of stones where workers had repaired the edge after a storm. I liked that detail because it made the place seem less like a picture in a book and more like somewhere people had to maintain.

We went upstairs after that. The stair rail was polished wood, and there were small brass numbers on the door frames. The upstairs gallery was indeed quieter, though a school group came through while we were looking at a wall of painted fragments. The paintings had been found in pieces, and the museum had placed them beside a drawing showing where they might have come from in a dining room. I almost said the colors were bright—no, not bright exactly, more like muted red and ochre, with a thin dark line around the leaves. Lena took a photo of the drawing, not the objects, because the display label asked visitors not to use flash.

2. The workshop table. Near the back of the gallery, a low display case held tools that had been found together in a small workshop. There was a stone weight, two iron blades, a wooden handle, and several tiny scraps of metal. The label said the scraps might have been left over from repairs, though it also said the exact work done there was uncertain. I appreciated that they did not pretend to know more than the evidence showed. Theo used the map to find the family house again, then spotted a symbol beside it that meant there was a touchable replica. The replica was a clay bowl with ridges around its edge. He turned it over carefully and said it felt heavier than he expected. A staff member told us it had been made from a scan of the original, so visitors could handle it without risking damage.

We stopped in the small cafe around one o’clock. I had tea and a cheese sandwich, Lena had soup, and Theo chose a biscuit shaped like a dinosaur even though there were no dinosaurs in the museum. From the table we could see the courtyard, where rainwater was collecting in a shallow channel beside a row of stones. After lunch we went back to the harbor room because Theo wanted to hear the recording once more. A toddler nearby kept saying, “Boat, boat,” and his father answered, “Yes, a very old boat.” That made us laugh softly. Before we left, I bought a postcard of the painted fragments and Lena bought a pencil for Theo. We had planned to stay an hour, but we had spent nearly four, and none of us felt rushed. On the walk back to the bus stop, Theo told us his favorite thing was the bowl because it was the only object he could touch. Mine was the harbor model, and Lena said hers was the doorway.
